title: Book 7, Chapter 23 — Nineteenth Year of the War—Battles in the Great Harbour—Retreat and Annihilation of the Athenian Army
paragraphs: The Athenians kept lingering where they were, doing nothing, and meanwhile Gylippus and Sicanus arrived at Syracuse. Sicanus had failed to win over Agrigentum: the party friendly to the Syracusans was driven out while he was still at Gela. Gylippus, however, brought with him not only a large force raised in Sicily but also the heavy infantry sent out in the spring from Peloponnese in the merchantmen, who had reached Selinus from Libya. A storm had carried these men to Libya. There they obtained two galleys and pilots from the Cyrenians, and on their way along the coast they sided with the Euesperitae and defeated the Libyans who were besieging them. From there they coasted on to Neapolis, a Carthaginian trading post and the nearest point to Sicily, only two days and a night away by sea. They crossed from there and came to Selinus. As soon as Gylippus arrived, the Syracusans prepared to attack the Athenians again, by land and sea at once. The Athenian generals saw a fresh army come to the help of the enemy, while their own affairs, far from improving, were growing worse every day, and the sickness among the soldiers distressed them above all. They now began to regret not having left earlier. Nicias no longer offered the same opposition, except to insist that there be no open vote, and they gave orders, as secretly as possible, for everyone to be ready to sail out of the camp at a given signal. All was at last ready and they were on the point of sailing away, when the moon, which was then full, was eclipsed. Most of the Athenians were deeply impressed by this and urged the generals to wait. Nicias, who was rather too much given to divination and practices of that kind, refused from that moment even to consider the question of leaving, until they had waited the thrice nine days that the soothsayers prescribed.

So the besiegers were condemned to stay where they were. The Syracusans got wind of what had happened and became more eager than ever to press them. The Athenians had now admitted themselves that they were no longer their superiors by sea or by land, since otherwise they would never have planned to sail away. The Syracusans also did not want the Athenians to settle in some other part of Sicily where they would be harder to deal with. They wanted to force them to fight at sea as soon as possible, in a position favorable to themselves. So they manned their ships and practiced for as many days as they thought enough. When the time came, on the first day they attacked the Athenian lines. A small force of heavy infantry and horse came out against them through certain gates. The Syracusans cut off some of the heavy infantry, routed the rest and pursued them to the lines. The entrance there was narrow, and the Athenians lost seventy horses and a few of the heavy infantry.

The Syracusans drew off their troops for that day. On the next they sailed out with a fleet of seventy-six ships and at the same time advanced with their land forces against the lines. The Athenians put out to meet them with eighty-six ships, came to close quarters and engaged. The Syracusans and their allies first defeated the Athenian center. Then they caught Eurymedon, the commander of the right wing, who was sailing out from the line closer to the land in order to surround the enemy. They caught him in the hollow and recess of the harbor, killed him and destroyed the ships with him. After that they chased the whole Athenian fleet before them and drove it ashore.

Gylippus saw the enemy’s fleet defeated and driven ashore beyond their stockades and camp. He ran down to the breakwater with some of his troops, to cut off the men as they landed and to make it easier for the Syracusans to tow off the ships, since the shore there was friendly ground. The Tyrrhenians who guarded this point for the Athenians saw them coming on in disorder. They advanced against them, attacked and routed their van, and threw it into the marsh of Lysimeleia. Afterward the Syracusan and allied troops arrived in greater numbers. The Athenians, afraid for their ships, came up too to help, engaged them, defeated them and pursued them some distance, and killed a few of their heavy infantry. They managed to save most of their ships and brought them down beside their camp. Eighteen, however, were taken by the Syracusans and their allies, and all the men on them were killed. The enemy tried to burn the rest by means of an old merchantman, which they filled with faggots and pine-wood, set on fire, and let drift down the wind, which blew straight toward the Athenians. The Athenians, alarmed for their ships, found ways to stop it and put it out, and to check the flames and the merchantman’s nearer approach. So they escaped the danger.

After this the Syracusans set up a trophy for the sea-fight, and for the heavy infantry whom they had cut off up at the lines, where they took the horses. The Athenians set up one for the rout of the foot soldiers driven into the marsh by the Tyrrhenians, and for their own victory with the rest of the army.

The Syracusans had now won a decisive victory at sea. Until then they had feared the reinforcement brought by Demosthenes. In consequence, the Athenians were deeply despondent, their disappointment was great, and their regret for having come on the expedition was greater still. These were the only cities they had yet encountered that were like their own in character, democracies like themselves, with ships and horses and of considerable size. They had been unable to divide them and bring them over by holding out the prospect of changes in their governments, or to crush them by their great superiority in force. They had failed in most of their attempts and were already perplexed. Now they had been defeated at sea, where defeat could never have been expected, and were plunged into deeper embarrassment than ever.

Meanwhile the Syracusans at once began to sail freely along the harbor, and they resolved to close up its mouth, so that the Athenians could not steal out in future, even if they wished. Indeed, the Syracusans no longer thought only of saving themselves. They also thought of how to prevent the enemy’s escape. They thought, and thought rightly, that they were now much the stronger, and that to conquer the Athenians and their allies by land and sea would win them great glory in Hellas. The rest of the Hellenes would then be freed at once, or released from their apprehension, since the remaining forces of Athens would be unable from then on to sustain the war that would be waged against her. The Syracusans, for their part, would be regarded as the authors of this deliverance and would be held in high admiration, not only by all men now living but also by posterity. Nor were these the only considerations that gave dignity to the struggle. They would conquer not only the Athenians but also their numerous allies. And they would not conquer alone, but with their companions in arms, commanding side by side with the Corinthians and Lacedaemonians, having offered their city to stand in the van of danger, and having been in great measure the pioneers of naval success.

Indeed, never before had so many peoples been assembled before a single city, except for the grand total gathered together in this war under Athens and Lacedaemon. The following were the states on either side that came to Syracuse to fight for or against Sicily, to help conquer or defend the island. What bound them together was not so much right or community of blood as interest or compulsion, as the case might be. The Athenians themselves, who are Ionians, went of their own free will against the Dorians of Syracuse. With them went the peoples who still speak the Attic language and use Athenian laws: the Lemnians, Imbrians and Aeginetans (that is, the then occupants of Aegina), who were their colonists. To these must be added the Hestiaeans dwelling at Hestiaea in Euboea. Of the rest, some joined the expedition as subjects of the Athenians, others as independent allies, others as mercenaries. Among the subjects paying tribute were the Eretrians, Chalcidians, Styrians and Carystians from Euboea; the Ceans, Andrians and Tenians from the islands; and the Milesians, Samians and Chians from Ionia. The Chians, however, joined as independent allies, paying no tribute but furnishing ships. Most of these were Ionians descended from the Athenians, except the Carystians, who are Dryopes. Although they were subjects and obliged to serve, they were still Ionians fighting against Dorians. Besides these there were men of Aeolic race: the Methymnians, subjects who provided ships, not tribute, and the Tenedians and Aenians, who paid tribute. These Aeolians were fighting against their Aeolian founders, the Boeotians in the Syracusan army, because they were obliged to. The Plataeans, the only native Boeotians opposed to Boeotians, did so out of a just quarrel. Of the Rhodians and Cytherians, both Dorians, the Cytherians were Lacedaemonian colonists, and they fought in the Athenian ranks against their Lacedaemonian countrymen with Gylippus. The Rhodians, Argives by race, were compelled to bear arms against the Dorian Syracusans and against their own colonists, the Geloans, who were serving with the Syracusans. Of the islanders around Peloponnese, the Cephallenians and Zacynthians accompanied the Athenians as independent allies, although their island position really left them little choice, because of the maritime supremacy of Athens. The Corcyraeans were not only Dorians but Corinthians, and they were openly serving against Corinthians and Syracusans, though they were colonists of the former and of the same race as the latter. They did so under a show of compulsion, but really out of free will, through hatred of Corinth. The Messenians, as they are now called, from Naupactus and from Pylos, then held by the Athenians, were taken with them to the war. There were also a few Megarian exiles, whose fate it was to be fighting now against the Megarian Selinuntines.

The engagement of the rest was more voluntary. What persuaded the Dorian Argives to join the Ionian Athenians in a war against Dorians was less the league than hatred of the Lacedaemonians and the immediate private advantage of each individual. The Mantineans and other Arcadian mercenaries were accustomed to go against whatever enemy was pointed out to them at the moment, and interest led them to regard the Arcadians serving with the Corinthians as just as much their enemies as anyone else. The Cretans and Aetolians also served for hire. The Cretans had joined the Rhodians in founding Gela, and they thus came to consent to fight for pay against their colonists instead of for them. There were also some Acarnanians serving for pay, although they came chiefly out of love for Demosthenes and goodwill to the Athenians, whose allies they were. All these lived on the Hellenic side of the Ionian Gulf. Of the Italiots, there were the Thurians and Metapontines, dragged into the quarrel by the stern necessities of a time of revolution. Of the Siceliots, there were the Naxians and the Catanians. Of the barbarians, there were the Egestaeans, who had called in the Athenians, most of the Sicels, and, from outside Sicily, some Tyrrhenian enemies of Syracuse and Iapygian mercenaries.

Such were the peoples serving with the Athenians. Against these the Syracusans had the Camarinaeans, their neighbors, and the Geloans, who live next to them. Then, passing over the neutral Agrigentines, there were the Selinuntines, settled on the farther side of the island. These inhabit the part of Sicily looking toward Libya. The Himeraeans came from the side toward the Tyrrhenian Sea; they were the only Hellenic inhabitants in that quarter, and the only people who came from there to help the Syracusans. Of the Hellenes in Sicily, the peoples named above joined in the war, all of them Dorians and independent. Of the barbarians, only the Sicels joined, that is, those who did not go over to the Athenians. Of the Hellenes outside Sicily, there were the Lacedaemonians, who provided a Spartan to take command and a force of Neodamodes or Freedmen, and of Helots; the Corinthians, who alone joined with both naval and land forces, together with their Leucadian and Ambraciot kinsmen; some mercenaries sent by Corinth from Arcadia; some Sicyonians forced to serve; and, from outside Peloponnese, the Boeotians. Compared with these foreign auxiliaries, however, the great Siceliot cities furnished more in every department: numbers of heavy infantry, ships and horses, and an immense multitude besides. And compared with all the rest put together, one may say, the Syracusans themselves provided more, both because of the greatness of their city and because they were in the greatest danger.

Such were the auxiliaries brought together on either side. All of them had joined by this time, and neither party received any later addition. It was no wonder, therefore, that the Syracusans and their allies thought it would win them great glory if they could follow up their recent victory in the sea-fight by capturing the whole Athenian armada, without letting it escape by sea or by land. They began at once to close up the Great Harbor, whose mouth is nearly a mile wide, with boats, merchant vessels and galleys moored broadside across it. They also made all their other arrangements for the event of the Athenians venturing to fight at sea again. There was, in fact, nothing small either in their plans or in their ideas.

The Athenians saw them closing up the harbor and were informed of their further designs, and they called a council of war. The generals and colonels assembled and discussed the difficulties of the situation. What pressed most was that they no longer had provisions for immediate use (they had sent word to Catana, in the belief that they were going away, not to send any), and that they would have none in future unless they could command the sea. They therefore resolved to evacuate their upper lines. They would enclose a small space close to the ships with a cross wall and garrison it; it would be just large enough to hold their stores and sick. Then they would man all the ships, seaworthy or not, with every man that could be spared from the rest of their land forces, and fight it out at sea. If they were victorious, they would go to Catana; if not, they would burn their ships, form in close order, and retreat by land to the nearest friendly place they could reach, Hellenic or barbarian. No sooner was this settled than it was carried out. They came down gradually from the upper lines and manned all their ships, compelling everyone of an age to be of any use to go on board. In this way they succeeded in manning about one hundred and ten ships in all. On these they embarked a number of archers and darters taken from the Acarnanians and the other foreigners, and they made all the other provisions that the nature of their plan allowed and the necessities behind it imposed. All was now nearly ready. Nicias saw that the soldiers were disheartened by their unprecedented and decisive defeat at sea, and that, because of the scarcity of provisions, they were eager to fight it out as soon as possible. He called them all together and addressed them first, speaking as follows:

“Soldiers of the Athenians and of the allies, we all have an equal interest in the coming struggle. Life and country are at stake for us quite as much as they can be for the enemy, since if our fleet wins the day, each of us can see his native city again, wherever that city may be. You must not lose heart or be like men without experience, who fail in a first attempt and ever afterward fearfully expect a future as disastrous. Let the Athenians among you, who have already had experience of many wars, and the allies, who have joined us in so many expeditions, remember the surprises of war. With the hope that fortune will not always be against us, prepare to fight again in a manner worthy of the great number that you see yourselves to be.

“Now, whatever we thought would be of service against the crush of ships in such a narrow harbor, and against the force upon the enemy’s decks, from which we suffered before, has all been considered with the helmsmen and, as far as our means allowed, provided for. A number of archers and darters will go on board, and a multitude of men that we should not have employed in an action in the open sea, where the weight of the ships would cripple our skill. But in the land-fight that we are now forced to make from shipboard, all this will be useful. We have also discovered the changes in construction that we must make to meet theirs. Against the thickness of their cheeks, which did us the greatest harm, we have provided grappling-irons. These will prevent an attacker from backing water after charging, if the soldiers on deck here do their duty. We are absolutely compelled to fight a land battle from the fleet, and it seems to be in our interest neither to back water ourselves nor to let the enemy do so, especially as the shore, except for the part of it held by our troops, is hostile ground.

“You must remember this and fight on as long as you can. You must not let yourselves be driven ashore. Once alongside, you must make up your minds not to part company until you have swept the heavy infantry from the enemy’s deck. I say this more to the heavy infantry than to the seamen, since it is more the business of the men on deck; and our land forces are even now on the whole the strongest. The sailors I advise, and at the same time implore, not to be too much daunted by their misfortunes, now that our decks are better armed and our ships more numerous. Bear in mind how well worth preserving is the pleasure of those of you who, through your knowledge of our language and imitation of our manners, were always considered Athenians, even though not so in reality. As such you were honored throughout Hellas, and you had your full share of the advantages of our empire, and more than your share of the respect of our subjects and of protection from ill treatment. You, therefore, with whom alone we freely share our empire, we now justly require not to betray that empire in its extremity. In scorn of the Corinthians, whom you have often conquered, and of the Siceliots, none of whom so much as presumed to stand against us when our navy was in its prime, we ask you to repel them, and to show that even in sickness and disaster your skill is more than a match for the fortune and vigor of anyone else.

“To the Athenians among you I add this reflection once more. You left behind you no more such ships in your docks as these, and no more heavy infantry in their flower. If you do anything but conquer, our enemies here will sail at once to Athens, and those of us who are left there will be unable to repel their assailants at home, who will be reinforced by these new allies. Here you will fall at once into the hands of the Syracusans (I need not remind you of the intentions with which you attacked them), and your countrymen at home will fall into the hands of the Lacedaemonians. Since the fate of both hangs on this single battle, stand firm now, if ever. Remember, each and all, that you who are now going on board are the army and navy of the Athenians, and all that is left of the state and the great name of Athens. In her defense, if any man has any advantage in skill or courage, now is the time for him to show it, and so to serve himself and save all.”

After this address Nicias at once gave orders to man the ships. Meanwhile Gylippus and the Syracusans could tell from the preparations they saw going on that the Athenians meant to fight at sea. They had also been told of the grappling-irons. Against these they made special provision, stretching hides over the prows and over much of the upper part of their ships, so that the irons, when thrown, would slip off without taking hold. All was now ready, and the generals and Gylippus addressed the men in the following terms:

“Syracusans and allies, we think most of you understand the glory of our past achievements and the no less glorious results at stake in the coming battle, or you would never have thrown yourselves with such ardor into the struggle. If anyone is not as fully aware of the facts as he ought to be, we will declare them to him. The Athenians came to this country first to conquer Sicily, and after that, if successful, Peloponnese and the rest of Hellas, since they already possessed the greatest empire yet known among the Hellenes, in present or former times. Here for the first time they found men who faced their navy, the navy that made them masters everywhere. You have already defeated them in the previous sea-fights, and in all likelihood you will defeat them again now. When men are once checked in what they consider their special excellence, their whole opinion of themselves suffers more than if they had never believed in their superiority. The unexpected shock to their pride makes them give way more than their real strength warrants, and this is probably the case with the Athenians now.

“With us it is different. The original estimate of ourselves, which gave us courage in the days of our unskillfulness, has been strengthened. To it has been added the conviction that we must be the best seamen of the time, if we have conquered the best. This has given every man among us a double measure of hope, and for the most part, where there is the greatest hope, there is also the greatest ardor for action. The means they have tried to find to combat us, by copying our armament, are familiar to our way of fighting and will be met with proper provisions. They will never be able to carry a number of heavy infantry on their decks, contrary to their custom, and a number of darters (born landsmen, one may say, Acarnanians and others, put afloat, who will not know how to discharge their weapons when they have to keep still), without hampering their ships and falling into confusion among themselves, through fighting not according to their own tactics. For they will gain nothing by the number of their ships. I say this to those of you who may be alarmed at having to fight against odds. A quantity of ships in a confined space will only be slower in executing the movements required, and most exposed to injury from our means of offense. Indeed, if you would know the plain truth, as we are credibly informed, the excess of their sufferings and the necessities of their present distress have made them desperate. They have no confidence in their force, but wish to try their fortune in the only way they can, either to force their passage and sail out, or after this to retreat by land, since it is impossible for them to be worse off than they are.

“The fortune of our greatest enemies has thus betrayed itself, and their disorder is what I have described. Let us engage in anger. Let us be convinced that, as between adversaries, nothing is more legitimate than to claim to sate the whole wrath of one’s soul in punishing the aggressor, and nothing is sweeter, as the proverb has it, than vengeance upon an enemy, which it will now be ours to take. That they are enemies, and mortal enemies, you all know, since they came here to enslave our country. If they had succeeded, they had in reserve for our men all that is most dreadful, for our children and wives all that is most dishonorable, and for the whole city the name that carries the greatest reproach. No one should therefore relent, or think it a gain if they go away without further danger to us. They will do that just the same, even if they get the victory. But if we succeed, as we may expect, in chastising them, and in handing down to all Sicily her ancient freedom, strengthened and confirmed, we shall have achieved no mean triumph. And the rarest dangers are those in which failure brings little loss and success the greatest advantage.”

After this address to the soldiers on their side, the Syracusan generals and Gylippus saw that the Athenians were manning their ships, and they immediately proceeded to man their own as well. Meanwhile Nicias was appalled by the position of affairs. He realized the greatness and nearness of the danger, now that they were on the point of putting out from shore. He thought, as men are apt to think in great crises, that when all has been done they still have something left to do, and that when all has been said they have not yet said enough. So he called on the captains again, one by one, addressing each by his father’s name and his own and that of his tribe. He adjured them not to belie their own personal renown or to obscure the hereditary virtues for which their ancestors were illustrious. He reminded them of their country, the freest of the free, and of the unfettered discretion allowed in it to all to live as they pleased. He added other arguments such as men would use at such a crisis, the kind that with little alteration are made to serve on all occasions alike, appeals to wives, children and national gods. He did not care whether they were thought commonplace, but invoked them loudly, in the belief that they would be of use in the consternation of the moment. Having thus admonished them, not as he would have wished, he felt, but as he could, Nicias withdrew and led the troops to the sea. He ranged them in as long a line as he was able, in order to help as far as possible in sustaining the courage of the men afloat. Meanwhile Demosthenes, Menander and Euthydemus, who took command on board, put out from their own camp and sailed straight to the barrier across the mouth of the harbor and to the passage left open, to try to force their way out.

The Syracusans and their allies had already put out with about the same number of ships as before. Some of these kept guard at the outlet; the rest were spread around the remainder of the harbor, to attack the Athenians from all sides at once. The land forces stood ready at the points where the ships might put in to shore. Sicanus and Agatharchus commanded the Syracusan fleet, each with a wing of the whole force, and Pythen and the Corinthians held the center. When the rest of the Athenians reached the barrier, the first shock of their charge overpowered the ships stationed there, and they tried to undo the fastenings. After this the Syracusans and allies bore down on them from every direction, and the fighting spread from the barrier over the whole harbor. It was more stubbornly contested than any of the earlier battles. On both sides the rowers showed great zeal in bringing up their ships at the boatswains’ orders, the helmsmen showed great skill in maneuvering, and each rivaled the others. Once ships were alongside, the soldiers on board did their best to keep the work on deck from being outdone by the rest. In short, every man strove to prove himself first in his own department. Many ships were engaged in a small space (these were the largest fleets ever to fight in the narrowest space, together little short of two hundred), so there were few regular attacks with the beak, since there was no chance to back water or to break the line. Collisions were more frequent, when one ship chanced to run foul of another while fleeing from a third or attacking it. As long as a ship was coming up to the charge, the men on the decks rained darts, arrows and stones on her. Once alongside, the heavy infantry tried to board each other’s vessels and fought hand to hand. In many places, because of the narrow room, a ship was charging an enemy on one side and being charged herself on another, and two or sometimes more ships had been forced to get entangled around one. This obliged the helmsmen to think of defense here and offense there, not of one thing at a time but of many on all sides. The huge din of so many ships crashing together not only spread terror but made the boatswains’ orders inaudible. The boatswains on both sides, in the discharge of their duty and in the heat of the conflict, shouted orders and appeals to their men without stopping. They urged the Athenians to force the passage out and, now if ever, to show their mettle and seize a safe return to their country. They told the Syracusans and their allies that it would be glorious to prevent the enemy’s escape and, by conquering, to exalt their own countries. The generals on both sides, moreover, if they saw anyone in any part of the battle backing ashore without being forced to, called to the captain by name and asked him a question. The Athenians asked whether they were retreating because they thought the thrice hostile shore more their own than the sea that had cost them so much labor to win. The Syracusans asked whether they were fleeing from the fleeing Athenians, whom they knew well to be eager to escape in any way they could.

Meanwhile the two armies on shore, while victory hung in the balance, were a prey to the most agonizing and conflicting emotions. The natives thirsted for more glory than they had already won, while the invaders feared to find themselves in even worse plight than before. Because everything the Athenians had was staked on their fleet, their fear for the outcome was like nothing they had ever felt, and their view of the struggle was necessarily as varied as the battle itself. They were close to the action and were not all looking at the same point at once. Some saw their friends winning, took courage, and called on heaven not to deprive them of safety. Others had their eyes on the losers; they wailed and cried aloud, and though only spectators, they were more overcome than the actual combatants. Others again were gazing at some spot where the battle was evenly disputed. As the struggle dragged on without decision, their swaying bodies reflected the agitation of their minds, and they suffered the worst agony of all, ever just within reach of safety or just on the point of destruction. In short, in that one Athenian army, as long as the sea-fight remained doubtful, every sound was to be heard at once: shrieks, cheers, “We win,” “We lose,” and all the other cries that a great host would necessarily utter in great peril. It was nearly the same with the men in the fleet. At last, after the battle had lasted a long while, the Syracusans and their allies put the Athenians to flight and chased them in open rout to the shore, with much shouting and cheering. The naval force, some one way and some another, ran ashore, all those not taken afloat, and rushed from their ships to the camp. The army was no longer divided but carried away by one impulse, and all deplored what had happened with shrieks and groans. Some ran down to help the ships, others to guard what was left of their wall, while the remaining and most numerous part already began to consider how they should save themselves. Indeed, the panic of that moment had never been surpassed. They now suffered very nearly what they had inflicted at Pylos. Then the Lacedaemonians, with the loss of their fleet, had also lost the men who had crossed over to the island; so now the Athenians had no hope of escaping by land, without the help of some extraordinary accident.

The sea-fight had been a severe one, and many ships and lives were lost on both sides. The victorious Syracusans and their allies now picked up their wrecks and dead, sailed off to the city, and set up a trophy. The Athenians, overwhelmed by their misfortune, never even thought of asking leave to take up their dead or their wrecks, but wished to retreat that very night. Demosthenes, however, went to Nicias and gave it as his opinion that they should man the ships they had left and make another effort to force their way out the next morning. He said they still had more ships fit for service than the enemy, for the Athenians had about sixty remaining against fewer than fifty of their opponents. Nicias was quite of his mind. But when they wished to man the ships, the sailors refused to go on board, so utterly overcome by their defeat that they no longer believed success was possible.

Accordingly they all now made up their minds to retreat by land. Meanwhile the Syracusan Hermocrates suspected their intention. He was impressed by the danger of letting a force of that size retire by land, settle in some other part of Sicily, and from there renew the war. So he went and stated his views to the authorities, and pointed out that they ought not to let the enemy get away by night; all the Syracusans and their allies should march out at once, block up the roads, and seize and guard the passes. The authorities were entirely of his opinion and thought it ought to be done. But they felt sure that the people, who had given themselves over to rejoicing and were taking their ease after a great battle at sea, would not easily be brought to obey. Besides, they were celebrating a festival, having a sacrifice to Heracles on that day, and most of them, in their rapture at the victory, had fallen to drinking at the festival. They would probably consent to anything sooner than to take up their arms and march out at that moment. For these reasons the magistrates thought the thing impracticable, and Hermocrates, finding he could do nothing more with them, now had recourse to a stratagem of his own. What he feared was that the Athenians might quietly get the start of them by passing the most difficult places during the night. So as soon as it was dusk he sent some friends of his own to the camp, with some horsemen. They rode up within earshot and called out to some of the men, as though they were well-wishers of the Athenians, telling them to tell Nicias (who in fact had some correspondents who informed him of what went on inside the town) not to lead the army off by night, since the Syracusans were guarding the roads, but to make his preparations at his leisure and to retreat by day. After saying this they departed. Their hearers informed the Athenian generals, who, not doubting the sincerity of this message, put off going for that night.

Since after all they had not set out at once, they now decided to stay the following day as well. This would give the soldiers time to pack, as well as they could, the most useful articles, and to start with only what was strictly necessary for their personal subsistence, leaving everything else behind. Meanwhile the Syracusans and Gylippus marched out and blocked up the roads through the country by which the Athenians were likely to pass. They kept guard at the fords of the streams and rivers, posting themselves so as to receive the Athenians and stop the army wherever they thought best. Their fleet sailed up to the beach and towed off the ships of the Athenians. A few were burned by the Athenians themselves, as they had intended. The rest, which had been thrown up on shore, the Syracusans lashed on to their own at their leisure, without anyone trying to stop them, and conveyed to the town.

After this, Nicias and Demosthenes thought that enough had been done by way of preparation, and the army moved off on the second day after the sea-fight. It was a lamentable scene, and not merely because they were retreating after losing all their ships, with their great hopes gone and themselves and the state in peril. In leaving the camp there were also things most grievous for every eye and heart to see. The dead lay unburied, and each man who recognized a friend among them shuddered with grief and horror. The living whom they were leaving behind, wounded or sick, were far more shocking to the living than the dead, and more to be pitied than those who had perished. These men fell to entreating and bewailing until their friends did not know what to do. They begged to be taken along and called loudly to each comrade or relative they could see. They hung on the necks of their tent-fellows as they departed and followed as far as they could. When their bodily strength failed them, they called again and again on heaven and shrieked aloud as they were left behind. So the whole army was filled with tears and distracted in this fashion, and found it not easy to go, even from an enemy’s land, where they had already suffered evils too great for tears and feared to suffer more in the unknown future before them. Dejection and self-condemnation were also rife among them. Indeed they could only be compared to a starved-out town, and no small one, escaping; the whole multitude on the march was not less than forty thousand men. All carried anything they could that might be of use. The heavy infantry and cavalry, contrary to their custom, carried their own provisions while under arms, in some cases for want of servants, in others through not trusting them, for they had long been deserting and now did so in greater numbers than ever. Even so they did not carry enough, as there was no longer food in the camp. Moreover, their disgrace in general, and the universality of their sufferings, though somewhat alleviated by being borne in company, were still felt at the moment as a heavy burden, especially when they contrasted the splendor and glory of their setting out with the humiliation in which it had ended. For this was by far the greatest reverse that ever befell a Hellenic army. They had come to enslave others, and were departing in fear of being enslaved themselves. They had sailed out with prayer and paeans, and now started back with omens directly contrary, traveling by land instead of by sea and trusting not in their fleet but in their heavy infantry. Nevertheless the greatness of the danger still impending made all this appear tolerable.

Nicias saw that the army was dejected and greatly altered. He passed along the ranks and encouraged and comforted them as far as was possible under the circumstances. In his earnestness, and in his anxiety that his words might reach as many as possible, he raised his voice higher and higher as he went from one company to another:

“Athenians and allies, even in our present position we must still hope on, since men have before now been saved from worse straits than this. You must not condemn yourselves too severely, either for your disasters or for your present undeserved sufferings. I myself am not stronger than any of you (indeed you see how I am in my sickness), and in the gifts of fortune, whether in private life or otherwise, I think I am the equal of anyone. Yet I am now exposed to the same danger as the meanest among you, although my life has been one of much devotion toward the gods, and of much justice and without offense toward men. I therefore still have a strong hope for the future, and our misfortunes do not terrify me as much as they might. Indeed we may hope that they will be lightened. Our enemies have had good fortune enough, and if any of the gods was offended at our expedition, we have already been amply punished. Others before us have attacked their neighbors and done what men will do, without suffering more than they could bear. We may now justly expect to find the gods kinder, for we have become fitter objects of their pity than of their jealousy. And then look at yourselves. Mark the numbers and efficiency of the heavy infantry marching in your ranks, and do not give way too much to despondency. Reflect that wherever you sit down you are yourselves a city at once, and that there is no other in Sicily that could easily resist your attack or expel you once you are established. The safety and order of the march are for yourselves to look to. Let each man think only that the spot where he may be forced to fight must be conquered and held as his country and stronghold. Meanwhile we shall hasten on our way night and day alike, as our provisions are scanty. If we can reach some friendly place of the Sicels, whom fear of the Syracusans still keeps true to us, you may at once consider yourselves safe. A message has been sent on to them with directions to meet us with supplies of food. To sum up, soldiers, be convinced that you must be brave, since there is no place near for your cowardice to take refuge in. If you now escape from the enemy, you may all see again what your hearts desire, and those of you who are Athenians will raise up again the great power of the state, fallen though it is. Men make the city, and not walls or ships without men in them.”

While he made this address, Nicias went along the ranks and brought back to their place any of the troops he saw straggling out of the line. Demosthenes did as much for his part of the army, addressing them in very similar words. The army marched in a hollow square, with the division under Nicias leading and that of Demosthenes following. The heavy infantry were on the outside, and the baggage-carriers and the bulk of the army in the middle. At the ford of the river Anapus they found a body of Syracusans and allies drawn up. They routed these, made good their passage and pushed on, harassed by the charges of the Syracusan horse and by the missiles of their light troops. That day they advanced about four miles and a half, and halted for the night upon a certain hill. The next day they started early and got on about two miles further. They descended into a place in the plain and encamped there, to get some food from the houses, since the place was inhabited, and to carry water on with them, because for many furlongs ahead, in the direction in which they were going, it was not plentiful. The Syracusans meanwhile went on and fortified the pass in front, where there was a steep hill with a rocky ravine on each side, called the Acraean cliff. The next day the Athenians advanced and found themselves impeded by the missiles and charges of the horse and darters of the Syracusans and allies, both very numerous. After fighting for a long while, they at length retired to the same camp. There they no longer had provisions as before, since it was impossible to leave their position because of the cavalry.

Early next morning they started afresh and forced their way to the hill that had been fortified. There they found the enemy’s infantry drawn up many shields deep to defend the fortification, the pass being narrow. The Athenians assaulted the work, but were met by a storm of missiles from the hill, which told with greater effect because it was steep. Unable to force the passage, they retreated again and rested. Meanwhile there were some claps of thunder and rain, as often happens toward autumn, which disheartened the Athenians still further, for they took all these things as omens of their approaching ruin. While they were resting, Gylippus and the Syracusans sent a part of their army to throw up works in their rear, on the way by which they had advanced. The Athenians, however, immediately sent some of their men and prevented them. After this they retreated more toward the plain and halted for the night. When they advanced the next day, the Syracusans surrounded and attacked them on every side and disabled many of them. They fell back if the Athenians advanced and came on if they retired, and in particular assaulted their rear, in the hope of routing them in detail and so striking a panic into the whole army. For a long while the Athenians persevered in this fashion, but after advancing four or five furlongs they halted to rest in the plain, and the Syracusans also withdrew to their own camp.

During the night Nicias and Demosthenes saw the wretched condition of their troops, who were now in want of every kind of necessary, and many of whom had been disabled in the numerous attacks of the enemy. They determined to light as many fires as possible and to lead off the army. They would no longer take the route they had intended, but would go toward the sea, in the direction opposite to the one the Syracusans were guarding. This whole route was leading the army not to Catana but to the other side of Sicily, toward Camarina, Gela, and the other Hellenic and barbarian towns in that quarter. They accordingly lit a number of fires and set out by night. Now all armies, and the greatest most of all, are liable to fears and alarms, especially when they are marching by night through an enemy’s country with the enemy near. The Athenians fell into one of these panics. The leading division, that of Nicias, kept together and got on a good way in front, while that of Demosthenes, comprising rather more than half the army, got separated and marched on in some disorder. By morning, however, they reached the sea. They got onto the Helorine road and pushed on to reach the river Cacyparis, intending to follow the stream up through the interior, where they hoped to be met by the Sicels whom they had sent for. When they arrived at the river, they found a Syracusan party there too, engaged in barring the passage of the ford with a wall and a palisade. They forced this guard, crossed the river, and went on to another river, called the Erineus, on the advice of their guides.

Meanwhile, when day came and the Syracusans and allies found that the Athenians were gone, most of them accused Gylippus of having let them escape on purpose. They pursued hastily by the road the Athenians had taken, which they had no difficulty in finding, and overtook them about dinner-time. They first came up with the troops under Demosthenes, who were behind, marching somewhat slowly and in disorder because of the night panic mentioned above. The Syracusans at once attacked and engaged them. The Syracusan horse surrounded them with more ease now that they were separated from the rest, and hemmed them in on one spot. The division of Nicias was five or six miles in front, for he led it more rapidly, thinking that under the circumstances their safety lay not in staying and fighting, unless obliged, but in retreating as fast as possible and fighting only when forced to. Demosthenes, on the other hand, was generally harassed more incessantly, since his post in the rear left him the first exposed to the enemy’s attacks. Now he found that the Syracusans were in pursuit, and instead of pushing on he stopped to form his men for battle. So he lingered until he was surrounded by his pursuers, and he and the Athenians with him were placed in the most distressing position. They were huddled into an enclosure with a wall all round it, a road on this side and on that, and olive-trees in great number, and missiles were showered in upon them from every quarter. The Syracusans had with good reason adopted this mode of attack in preference to fighting at close quarters, since to risk a struggle with desperate men was now more to the advantage of the Athenians than of themselves. Besides, their success had now become so certain that they began to spare themselves a little, so as not to be cut off in the moment of victory. They thought, too, that as things stood they would be able in this way to subdue and capture the enemy.

In fact, they plied the Athenians and allies all day long from every side with missiles, until at length they saw that they were worn out with their wounds and other sufferings. Then Gylippus and the Syracusans and their allies made a proclamation, offering liberty to any of the islanders who chose to come over to them, and some few cities went over. Afterwards a capitulation was agreed upon with Demosthenes for all the rest: they were to lay down their arms, on condition that no one would be put to death, whether by violence, by imprisonment, or by want of the necessaries of life. Upon this they surrendered, six thousand in all, laying down all the money in their possession, which filled the hollows of four shields, and were immediately conveyed by the Syracusans to the town.

Meanwhile Nicias with his division arrived that day at the river Erineus, crossed over, and posted his army on some high ground on the other side. The next day the Syracusans overtook him and told him that the troops under Demosthenes had surrendered, and invited him to follow their example. Nicias did not believe it and asked for a truce to send a horseman to see. The messenger returned with the news that they had surrendered, and Nicias sent a herald to Gylippus and the Syracusans. He said that he was ready to agree with them, on behalf of the Athenians, to repay whatever money the Syracusans had spent on the war, if they would let his army go; and until the money was paid he offered to give Athenians as hostages, one for every talent. The Syracusans and Gylippus rejected this proposal, and attacked this division as they had the other, standing all round and plying them with missiles until the evening. The troops of Nicias were as miserably short of food and necessaries as their comrades had been. Nevertheless they waited for the quiet of the night to resume their march. But as they were taking up their arms, the Syracusans noticed it and raised their paean. The Athenians, finding that they were discovered, laid their arms down again, except for about three hundred men who forced their way through the guards and went on during the night as they were able.

As soon as it was day Nicias put his army in motion. As before, the Syracusans and their allies pressed him, pelting the Athenians from every side with missiles and striking them down with javelins. The Athenians pushed on for the Assinarus. The attacks made on them from every side by a numerous cavalry and the swarm of other troops impelled them, and they fancied they would breathe more freely once across the river. They were driven on also by exhaustion and craving for water. Once there they rushed in, and all order was at an end. Each man wanted to cross first, and the enemy’s attacks made it difficult to cross at all. Forced to huddle together, they fell against and trod down one another. Some died at once on the javelins, others got entangled together and stumbled over the baggage, unable to rise again. Meanwhile the opposite bank, which was steep, was lined by the Syracusans, who showered missiles down on the Athenians, most of them drinking greedily and heaped together in disorder in the hollow bed of the river. The Peloponnesians also came down and butchered them, especially those in the water. It was spoiled at once, but they went on drinking it just the same, mud and all, bloody as it was, and most even fought to have it.

At last many dead lay piled one upon another in the stream, and part of the army had been destroyed at the river, and the few who escaped from there were cut off by the cavalry. Then Nicias surrendered himself to Gylippus, whom he trusted more than the Syracusans. He told him and the Lacedaemonians to do what they liked with him, but to stop the slaughter of the soldiers. After this Gylippus immediately gave orders to take prisoners. The rest were brought together alive, except for a large number secreted by the soldiery, and a party was sent in pursuit of the three hundred who had got through the guard during the night, and who were now taken with the rest. The number of the enemy collected as public property was not considerable, but the number secreted was very large, and all Sicily was filled with them, since no convention had been made for them as for those taken with Demosthenes. Besides this, a large portion were killed outright, the carnage being very great, and not exceeded by any in this Sicilian war. In the numerous other encounters on the march, not a few had also fallen. Nevertheless many escaped, some at the moment, others after serving as slaves and running away later. These found refuge at Catana.

The Syracusans and their allies now mustered, took up the spoils and as many prisoners as they could, and went back to the city. The rest of their Athenian and allied captives they deposited in the quarries, this seeming the safest way of keeping them. But Nicias and Demosthenes were butchered, against the will of Gylippus, who thought it would be the crown of his triumph if he could take the enemy’s generals to Lacedaemon. As it happened, one of them, Demosthenes, was one of her greatest enemies, on account of the affair of the island and of Pylos; while the other, Nicias, was for the same reasons one of her greatest friends, owing to his exertions to procure the release of the prisoners by persuading the Athenians to make peace. For these reasons the Lacedaemonians felt kindly toward him, and it was on this that Nicias himself mainly relied when he surrendered to Gylippus. But some of the Syracusans who had been in correspondence with him were afraid, it was said, that he would be put to the torture and trouble their success by his revelations. Others, especially the Corinthians, were afraid that, being wealthy, he would escape by means of bribes and live to do them further mischief. These persuaded the allies and had him put to death. This, or something like it, was the cause of the death of a man who, of all the Hellenes in my time, least deserved such a fate, seeing that the whole course of his life had been regulated with strict attention to virtue.

The Syracusans treated the prisoners in the quarries harshly at first. They were crowded into a narrow hole with no roof to cover them. By day the heat of the sun and the stifling closeness of the air tormented them, and then the nights, which came on autumnal and chilly, made them ill by the violence of the change. Besides, for want of room they had to do everything in the same place, and the bodies of those who died of their wounds, of the change in temperature, or of similar causes were left heaped together one upon another, so that intolerable stenches arose. Hunger and thirst never ceased to afflict them, for during eight months each man was given only half a pint of water and a pint of corn a day. In short, no single suffering to be expected by men thrust into such a place was spared them. For some seventy days they lived there all together. After that all were sold, except the Athenians and any Siceliots or Italiots who had joined in the expedition. The total number of prisoners taken would be difficult to state exactly, but it cannot have been less than seven thousand.

This was the greatest Hellenic achievement of any in this war, or, in my opinion, in Hellenic history: at once most glorious to the victors and most calamitous to the conquered. They were beaten at all points and altogether. All that they suffered was great. They were destroyed, as the saying is, with a total destruction: their fleet, their army, everything was destroyed, and few out of many returned home. Such were the events in Sicily.
